title: "Markdown cheatsheet"
callout-appearance: default
from: markdown+emoji
---

Below, you find an overview of basic and advanced Markdown formatting styles you can use in Obsidian.

You don't need to know all of this. Use this page as a reference and come back to it when needed.

## Basics

### Headers

```markdown
# Heading 1
## Heading 2
### Heading 3
#### Heading 4
##### Heading 5
```

### Emphasis

```markdown
**Bold text**

*Italic text*

***Bold and italic text***

==Highlighted text==
```

Hotkeys: Ctrl/Cmd + B for bold and Ctrl/Cmd + I for italic.

### Lists

```markdown
- this is
- an unordered
- list
```

```markdown
1. this is
2. an ordered
3. list
```

### Task lists (checkboxes)

```markdown
- [ ] An open task
- [x] A completed task
```

Hotkey: Ctrl/Cmd + L turns a line into a task.

### External links

```markdown
[A link to Google](https://google.com)
```

Hotkey: Ctrl/Cmd + K.

You can embed links by putting an `!` before the link. This works for some web content but is especially helpful for videos, e.g.

```markdown
![](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E6ySG7xYgjY)
```

### Internal links

Internal links are links that link to other files in your Obsidian vault. As soon as you start typing `[[]]`, Obsidian will suggest files you can link to.

```markdown
[[Markdown cheatsheet]]
[[Markdown cheatsheet|A different display name for the link]]
```

Also here, you can add `!` to embed the content. This is useful to embed PDFs, images, but also other note content, e.g.

```markdown
![[Markdown cheatsheet]]
```

You can also link to specific sections of another file using `#`:

```markdown
[[Markdown cheatsheet#Headers|Check the header section]]
```

## Advanced

### Formulas

You can use the LaTeX syntax for formulas. Use `$` to enclose inline equations and `$$` for blocked equations.

```markdown
This $\pi = \pi$ is an inline equation
```

```markdown
$$
\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2}
$$
```

### Horizontal lines

```markdown
I add a horizontal line

---

between these two paragraphs
```

### Quotes

```markdown
> A wise woman said this thing
```

### Footnotes

```markdown
This is a sentence with a footnote. [^1]
[^1]: This is the footnote text
```

### Callouts

There are different types of callout boxes, the default is a note:

```markdown
> [!note]
> Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet
```

You can **change the title**:

```markdown
> [!note] This has a custom title
> Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet
```

You can make the callout **foldable** by adding a `+` (unfolded by default) or `-` (folded by default) after the type:

```markdown
> [!note]- This has a folded callout
> Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet
```

Depending on what you put in the `[]`, the callout will look differently. Other types are:

```markdown
> [!abstract]
> [!info]
> [!todo]
> [!tip]
> [!success]
> [!help]
> [!warning]
> [!failure]
> [!danger]
> [!bug]
> [!example]
> [!quote]
```

### Inline code

```markdown
This `word` is formatted like code because of the backticks.
```

### Code blocks

Code blocks start and end with 3 backticks. After the 3 backticks in the first line, add the language (e.g. R, python, cpp, ...)

````markdown
```R
# This is an R code block
library(tidyverse)
my_data <- read_csv("my_data.csv")
```
````
